slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1870 and 1880 censuses interpolated to November 1876, men 21+ outside the former Confederate states, Black men included under the Fifteenth Amendment; calibrated to certified returns (the Electoral Commission's counts for the three disputed states).

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: No women could vote for president in 1876; women 21+ shown for population only.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1870 and 1880 censuses interpolated to 1876, white adults in the former Confederate states, all voting by popular vote; calibrated to certified returns, which in Florida, Louisiana and South Carolina were disputed and settled by the Electoral Commission.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1870 and 1880 censuses interpolated to 1876, Black adults in the former Confederate states; Black men voted under the Fifteenth Amendment, with federal troops still in South Carolina, Louisiana and Florida, but organized violence and intimidation (the Mississippi Plan, the red shirts) cut their vote across much of the South.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1870 and 1880 censuses interpolated to 1876, foreign-born white men not yet naturalized; many Midwestern, Western and Southern states let declarant aliens vote, elsewhere only naturalized men could.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1876 comes out as it did: Hayes wins, 185–184. The closest state was South Carolina, which went to Hayes by 0.5 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1870 and 1880 census counts interpolated to 1876 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1876 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 13.6 million more adults vote. Tilden wins, 56–313. The closest call is Alabama, which holds for Tilden by 2.5 points. Tilden wins in 98 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1876.
howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I cannot vote myself, though I take an interest in what the men decide tomorrow. My household depends on how the business fares under whoever wins.
south-white.controlQuote: I cannot vote myself, though I take an interest in what the men decide tomorrow. My household depends on how the business fares under whoever wins.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I cannot vote myself, though I wish I could make my voice heard on these matters troubling our farms and the nation.
women.controlQuote: I cannot vote myself, though I wish I could make my voice heard on these matters troubling our farms and the nation.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: I'll vote the Republican ticket. The general's honest enough, and we can't let the South slip back. Though Lord knows there's been plenty of waste in Washington these past years.

questions: Election Day is Tuesday. Can this person vote, how likely are they to vote, and if they vote, for whom?
A neighbour asks what this person will do on Tuesday, 7 November. Will they cast a ballot for president, and for which candidate?
